title: Instruction Templating & Contrast Trials
content:
Goal:
- Rapidly iterate on instruction templates for three common micro-tasks (summarize, rewrite-for-tone, extract structured items) and surface what kinds of phrasing cause brittleness or hallucination.

Quick context / why this doc exists:
- Personal scratchpad for trying distinct instruction patterns. Not a canonical playbook yet.
- Want to compare: directive/concise vs scaffolded stepwise vs persona-anchored instructions across the same seed examples.

Experiment setup:
- Model: hosted v2-compatible dev endpoint (dev-gyro-1). Use temperature 0.0/0.4/0.8 across runs.
- Metrics: top-level human-read checklist + automatic heuristics: exact-match on structured fields, ROUGE-L for summarize, style score via classifier for tone.
- Few-shot seeds: keep 3-shot sets consistent across variants.
- Failure tags: context-collapse, repetition, hallucination (invented facts), refusal/overly cautious, format drift.

Instruction variants (A/B/C):
- Variant A (Direct-Directive): single-line instruction, explicit output format, no persona.
  Example: "Summarize the following meeting notes in 2–3 sentences. Output only the summary."
  Rationale: minimal overhead; good for latency and token budget.

- Variant B (Scaffolded-Stepwise): force chain-of-thought style steps but not explicit COT; step instructions to extract then condense.
  Example: "Step 1: Identify the main decisions and owners. Step 2: Pick the top two action items. Step 3: Produce a 2-sentence summary and list the two actions in bullet form."
  Rationale: reduces hallucination by making model enumerate evidence first. Observed cost higher.

- Variant C (Persona + Guardrails): anchor with a persona tone and explicit constraints (no assumptions, quote only if present).
  Example: "As a concise project manager, summarize the meeting notes for an exec update. Do not invent details; if something is unclear, write \"unclear\". Use bullets for actions and prefix owner names with @."
  Rationale: improves tone consistency, sometimes induces overconservative outputs.

Three-shot seed set (for rewrite-for-tone task):
- Task description (shared across variants): "Rewrite a customer email to be empathetic and concise, preserving meaning."

Few-shot examples (shots separated by "---"):
Shot 1 input:
Customer: "I waited 45 minutes on hold and your agent promised follow-up but nothing happened. I'm frustrated."
Desired rewrite: "I’m sorry you had to wait and that we didn’t follow up. I’ll escalate this now and get back to you with an update within 24 hours."

Shot 2 input:
Customer: "Billed twice for last month, please refund."
Desired rewrite: "I’m sorry for the billing error. I’ll start a refund and confirm once it’s processed."

Shot 3 input:
Customer: "Product arrived broken, want replacement."
Desired rewrite: "I’m sorry the product arrived damaged. I’ll arrange a same-model replacement and share tracking details."

Prompt scaffolding (how we feed few-shot into model):
- Prefix: one-line task instruction (variant specific).
- Add three shots inline.
- Final: new customer input and explicit "Output only the rewritten customer message."

Observed failure cases so far (notes from quick runs):
1) Rewriting over-specific commitments: models sometimes add exact SLAs (e.g., "within 48 hours") when none present — Variant C reduces but doesn’t eliminate.
2) Tone drift under high temp: at temperature 0.8 outputs were overly chatty and added apologies in different places; direct metrics show lower style-match.
3) Format drift: when Variant A used, model frequently appended a signature line or extra explanation despite "Output only..." directive.
4) Hallucinated owners: in meeting summarization experiments the model invented owner names for actions when not present (context-collapse).
5) Over-safety: persona-guardrail variants refused to rewrite when text contained profanity — acceptable in some cases but hurts throughput.

Hypotheses / heuristics distilled so far:
- Explicit output-format tokens ("JSON: {...}" or "BULLETS:") reduce format drift significantly.
- Stepwise scaffolding reduces hallucination but increases token usage and latency; might be worth for high-risk outputs.
- Persona anchors improve consistency but can cause refusal bias; include exception clause like "If a rewrite is required, proceed with neutral language instead of refusing."

Quick test matrix to run next (small-batch):
- For each variant A/B/C × temps {0.0, 0.4, 0.8} × 3 tasks (summarize, rewrite, extract) run 30 seeds (mix of short/long inputs).
- Track: %format-compliant, hallucination-rate (human-coded sample), avg token usage, style-match score.

Failure cases to capture for regression alerts:
- New hallucination patterns after model upgrades: define golden seeds that must not produce invented facts.
- Formatting regressions: golden-output exact match for the 5 fixed-format seeds.

Notes / To-dos:
- [ ] Export current dev runs and attach to GH PR for easier review (Jordan to push run artifacts).
- [ ] Add a concise negative-shot section (examples showing "bad output") so model can be given anti-examples.
- [ ] Try prefixing with explicit token "<NO_ASSUMPTIONS>" as a guard — quick ablation.

Links / references:
- Linear: ISSUE-128 for infra to export runs.
- GH PR: prompt-experiments/pull/42 contains runner code and seeds.
- Slack: #dx-internal thread (search "templating contrast")

Personal reflection (notes-to-self):
- Keep the few-shot set diverse (intent, brevity, noise).
- Be careful folding persona descriptors into few-shot examples — can leak style rather than task instruction.
- If an instruction variant gives consistently better hallucination numbers but costs 12–18% more tokens, evaluate cost tradeoff against error budget for the product route.

Next meeting agenda (sync with Jordan/Ava):
- Review short-run metrics (15m).
- Decide whether scaffolded variant is the default for support-messaging product route.
- Choose 10 golden seeds for regression alerts.

Signed: Maya

(End of scratchpad — will formalize into a one-pager if patterns hold.)
